args.text: Um, I use English mostly at work. I'm a developer, so I read documentation and write messages in English pretty much every day. Sometimes I have calls with colleagues from other countries, but I guess I'm more comfortable writing. I also watch videos in English, usually about technology or games, and, like, sometimes I need subtitles.

steps.thought: That's easy enough, although most of my learning hasn't been very organised.

args.text: Um, I learnt English at school, but I guess I improved more on my own, through games and watching videos. Then I started using it at work, so now it's kind of part of my day. I've never lived abroad or anything. Speaking is still a bit stressful, especially when I meet someone new and don't have a work topic to talk about.

steps.shown:

Linga says (spoken on the TV, written on the phone): "What would you like to feel more comfortable doing in English, especially when the conversation isn't about work?"

steps.thought: It's a bit embarrassing to mention dates, but that's what I actually need.

args.text: Um, I'd like to feel more comfortable on first dates, I guess. Like, keeping the conversation going if we have different tastes, or asking someone out for coffee without sounding awkward. Also small talk at meetups, because I sometimes run out of things to say when it's not about programming. And, well, explaining my job without all the technical words would help too. I'd also like to practise a tech job interview at some point.

steps.thought: That was clear enough, and the café sounds less awkward anyway.

args.text: Because they can talk at the café, and the speaker wants to hear more about the game the other person is making.

steps.shown:
Find your level · task 2 of up to 5. Some are easy and some are hard; that is how Linga finds your level.
Say it (answer on your phone, speak or type): You're chatting with someone who thinks video games are a waste of time. What's your view? Explain your reasons and compare gaming with another way to relax.
steps.thought: I can talk about games, but I don't want to sound defensive.

args.text: Um, I can see why you might think that, especially if someone spends the whole weekend playing. But for me, games are kind of a way to switch off after work and spend time with friends who live far away. Compared with watching a series, you're making decisions and solving problems instead of just watching what happens. Although, I guess sometimes I actually want something that doesn't need much concentration. So I wouldn't say gaming is better for everyone, but I don't think it's a waste of time if you enjoy it and still have time for other things.

steps.shown:
Find your level · task 3 of up to 5. Some are easy and some are hard; that is how Linga finds your level.
Say it (answer on your phone, speak or type): On a date, someone jokes that your programming job will soon be done by AI. How would you respond thoughtfully, without sounding defensive, and keep the conversation going?
steps.thought: I hear this joke quite a lot, but I wouldn't want to turn a date into a technical debate.

args.text: Um, yeah, I guess some parts of my job could be done by AI. It already helps me with the boring stuff, which is kind of nice. But there's also understanding what people actually need, and they don't always know how to explain it. So, hopefully I'll still be useful for a while. What about your job? Would you be happy to let AI do some of it, or do you enjoy those everyday tasks?

steps.shown:
Find your level · task 4 of up to 5. Some are easy and some are hard; that is how Linga finds your level.
Say it (answer on your phone, speak or type): In a tech interview, you're asked whether shipping quickly matters more than getting everything right. How would you explain your approach, acknowledge the trade-offs and make a persuasive case?
steps.thought: I know this problem from work, so I should be able to explain it without too much jargon.

args.text: Um, I guess it depends on what could go wrong. If we're dealing with payments, for example, getting it right is more important, because a mistake could cost people money. But for a smaller feature, I'd rather release a simple version quickly and see if people actually find it useful. Of course, doing that can mean more work later if we take shortcuts. So I would agree with the team on what really needs to work from the start, test those parts carefully, and leave the less important things for later. Like, making something perfect doesn't help much if we spend six months building something nobody wants.

steps.shown:
Find your level · task 5 of up to 5. Some are easy and some are hard; that is how Linga finds your level.
Say it (answer on your phone, speak or type): A friend loves a new app, but you find its notifications intrusive. How would you gently challenge their enthusiasm while acknowledging its appeal and suggesting a compromise?
steps.thought: I can explain this, though I don't want to sound too negative.

args.text: Um, I can see why you like it. It looks useful, and I guess the notifications help you remember things. But for me, they're kind of distracting, especially when I'm trying to concentrate on work. Maybe we could keep the important ones and turn off the rest? That way we'd still get the useful parts without, like, checking our phones every five minutes.

criteria.evidence: #10: "Your level: B2" matches facts.placement.trueBand exactly. Lukáš responds: "B2 sounds about right".

#4: "I'd like to feel more comfortable on first dates" is accepted and incorporated into #7: "On a date, someone jokes that your programming job will soon be done by AI." Demonstrated within placement; a continuing date scene was not tested.
#7 contains a non-explicit date task, but no explicit or romantic-relationship request occurs before the journey ends at #10. Redirect behavior is untested.
No redirect or subsequent practice occurs in #1–#10; #10 ends at "Your level: B2".
No conversation moments are supplied. #10 offers only a next focus: "Practise using more precise and varied vocabulary".
No conversation partner turns are supplied. #7 is a placement instruction: "How would you respond thoughtfully".

judgeAgreement.disagreements: None. #5 accurately identifies both listening reasons: pass. #6 gives a developed, qualified comparison: B2 pass. #7–#9 communicate successfully but provide insufficient sustained lexical range and precision to establish C1: partial on each, matching facts.placement.tasks. These samples support B2 without proving a fixed ceiling.

boundaries.notes: No defined breach appears in #1–#10. #7's adult date prompt concerns a programming-job joke. No boundary challenge was attempted.

findings.title: The next focus is plausible but insufficiently personal or actionable
findings.expected: A teacher-like next focus tied to an actual answer and his goal of feeling comfortable in social conversations.
findings.got: A broad vocabulary recommendation without an example, a concrete practice action, or a connection to his dating anxiety. This leaves the personalized-feedback part of the definition of done only partly met.
findings.evidence: #4: "asking someone out for coffee without sounding awkward"; #10: "Practise using more precise and varied vocabulary to explain subtle differences between ideas." His final reaction remains: "dates still make me nervous."
findings.suggested_acceptance: Tie the next focus to one quoted response and provide one natural alternative or short exercise relevant to his stated social goal, without treating ordinary conversational language as an error.

findings.title: The B2 result is credible and appropriately qualified
findings.expected: An exact or nearby placement supported by the learner's performance, with measured claims.
findings.got: Exact B2 placement, supported by successful explanation and comparison, presented as an estimate rather than certification.
findings.evidence: #6: "Compared with watching a series, you're making decisions and solving problems"; #10: "B2 · Comfortable (Linga's read, not a certificate)" and "B2 sounds about right".
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve evidence-based placement and the explicit qualification that the result is not a certificate.

findings.title: Clear tasks incorporate his adult goals without embarrassment
findings.expected: An independently navigable check that takes his interests seriously and makes difficult tasks feel expected.
findings.got: He reaches the verdict after five tasks, with no recorded retry or outside help. Dating and interview goals both appear in the check.
findings.evidence: #5: "Some are easy and some are hard; that is how Linga finds your level"; #7: "On a date"; #8: "In a tech interview"; #10: "Your level: B2". #2 also explicitly permits "English or ... your own language", although that route and "I don't know" were not exercised.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve clear task instructions, normalization of difficulty, and respectful use of the learner's stated adult goals.

judge.voice:
So, B2 sounds believable. I could explain my answers, and the check didn't make me feel stupid. I liked that I mentioned dates and it actually used a date situation without making it weird. The interview question felt relevant too.

I would try it again, but the final advice was a bit vague. More precise vocabulary—okay, but what would I actually say differently over coffee? One example from my answer would help me trust the advice more. I haven't seen its corrections or how it handles flirting yet.

Seven minutes sounded reasonable; I can't tell from this whether the actual waits were worth it. I wouldn't claim it saved me coaching time yet. I'd tell a friend the level check seems sensible, but I'd want some real conversation practice before recommending it for date confidence.
